plos-pone-0005385: Facial clefts are common birth defects with strong genetic roots. Jugessur and team genotyped 1536 SNPs in 357 candidate genes across two Scandinavian cleft studies. The large scan hunts fetal risk factors. Genes of the developing face, mapped at unprecedented group scale.
plos-pone-0005485: Even archaea, life's simplest cells, may expect daily cycles. Whitehead and team found daily synced readying conduct in archaea. The finding pushes living clocks to life's deepest branches. Clock at the dawn of life, in single cells, waiting as a universal living plan.
plos-pone-0005585: Fibrosis is hard to diagnose without biopsies. Muzard and team made a skin protein-targeted imaging agent based on a platelet sensor mimic. The peptidomimetic enables non-invasive fibrosis finding. Seeing scars without cutting, unit by unit, tiny imaging for chronic sickness monitoring.
plos-pone-0005685: Immune-lacking patients need tuned antibody care. Figge built a chance immune-response model to tune defense proteins swap. The math tailors dosing, copying defense swap parts by chance, in mathematical care for rare immune troubles: systems biology serving patients through dosing by model, complex tuning systems in the clinic applied.
plos-pone-0005785: Ultramicroscopy images large transparent samples in 3D. Leischner and team studied its resolution and field of view. The technique enables whole-sample imaging. Seeing big biology in 3D, resolved, histological clearing plus optics, microscopy's resolution limits probed, large samples in fine detail.
plos-pone-0006385: Tumors that hide from T cells are hard to kill. Li and team found B7 boosts T-cell attack on TAP-lacking tumors. Adding TAP1 makes the trick work better. Unmasking hidden tumors, for immune therapy — TAP loss usually blocks killing, but B7 breaks the block.
plos-pone-0006485: Deep-sea mussels blur species lines. Faure and team traced gene flow between two mixing mussels. The split is still leaking — evolution in the dark, mapped, at boiling vents. Multi-gene study, with merging theory used: split dated, gene flow tested, two species, one story.
plos-pone-0006585: Depression's brain mix, mapped. Sequeira and team linked glutamate and GABA gene shifts to suicide and depression. Beyond serotonin, new clues — sadness' map, drawn, with global readouts. Major public health, disease path in view: brain chemicals weighed, new targets, hope for treatments.
plos-pone-0009385: A drug-resistant staph germ known as livestock-associated MRSA has turned up in farm animals, farmers, and meat. This Dutch study asks whether it is spreading to people with no direct animal contact in pig-dense regions. By testing residents near intensive pig farms, the researchers measured how far the resistant bug reaches into ordinary communities — a key question for public health beyond the farm gate.
plos-pone-0009485: Benign thyroid tumors affect about 5% of adults, and many carry rearrangements on chromosome 19. This study finds those rearrangements switch on two microRNA gene clusters, flooding the tumor with tiny regulatory RNAs. The paper identifies a molecular signature of these common tumors — and a mechanism by which a chromosome shuffle rewires a cell.
plos-pone-0009585: When dendritic cells sense bacterial toxin, they sound the immune alarm — and the protein JunB helps turn up the volume. This study shows JunB, acting through the NF-kB pathway, drives production of inflammatory signals. The paper maps a control point in the immune system's first response to infection.
plos-pone-0010385: Ventilators can injure lungs by overstretching their lining. This study stretches rat lung cells and finds MAPk signaling controls how leaky the barrier becomes. The paper identifies a molecular dial on ventilator-induced lung damage, with implications for critical care.
plos-pone-0010485: New species arise through genetic rewiring — but which changes matter? This study analyzes genetic shifts during fruit fly speciation. The paper probes the DNA of the origin of species. The analysis hunts the genetic sparks that ignite new species from old.
plos-pone-0010585: Gene therapy viruses can hide in the liver for months, ignored by the immune system. This mouse study shows the signal protein LIGHT can flush out that lingering antigen — but the cleanup also inflames the liver. Help comes with harm. The paper captures immunity's double edge.
plos-pone-0010685: Malaria vaccines protect in trials but fail in the field. This meta-analysis of 1,916 immunization studies asks why. The paper builds a new immunological model. The answer could finally rescue the global malaria vaccine effort after decades of repeated failure.
plos-pone-0010785: Marine iguanas host gut microbes that trade genes. This study finds phylogenetic evidence for lateral gene transfer inside the iguana intestine. The paper extends this gene-swapping beyond mammals. The finding broadens microbiome science to reptiles and the sea. The sea lizards rewrite the textbooks.
plos-pone-0010885: More people now seek therapy online — are they typical patients? This study compares internet-clinic anxiety and depression cases with national survey and outpatient data. The paper checks representativeness. The findings validate digital mental-health care. The online patients look reassuringly ordinary.
plos-pone-0010985: A sluggish heartbeat can run in families. This study probes thirteen mutant versions of the SCN5A sodium channel to uncover how they cause sick sinus syndrome. The paper reveals several distinct failure mechanisms. The work guides diagnosis and treatment of inherited rhythm disorders.
plos-pone-0011085: Prion diseases hide behind the blood-brain barrier. This study designs liposome-siRNA-peptide complexes that cross the barrier and slash prion protein in neurons and infected cultures. The paper delivers a brain-penetrating therapy. The approach could treat Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. The therapy strikes the disease at its root.
plos-pone-0011185: Sheep traded between farms carry disease with them. This study models infectious-disease transmission through sheep movement networks. The paper reveals how contact networks drive outbreaks. The finding informs livestock-disease control. The targeted control blocks the highest-risk animal movements first.
plos-pone-0011285: City shores teem with distinctive germs. This study surveys germ communities in coastal city watersheds and builds new pollution indicators from them. The paper offers a monitoring tool. The finding aids water-quality work. The managed waters stay safe for swimmers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1285:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 20 July 1945. It joins the British run of staff papers in the volume. London's chiefs advised their own team in the same form their American partners used across the hall.

The British services faced a world-wide bill: occupation in Europe, war in Asia, and fleets on every sea. Their papers sorted those claims for the envoys. This one dates from the first week's close. It is the British military house's view at that point, preserved through the allies' habit of sharing staff paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1385:
Stanisław Mikołajczyk, deputy prime minister of Poland, set down a memorandum on 24 July 1945. Mikołajczyk had led Poland's government in exile in London before joining the new Warsaw government that summer. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Poland's fate was the sharpest moral question at Potsdam: its borders moved west, and its government was remade under Soviet eyes. Mikołajczyk stood between the worlds, a democrat inside a regime he did not control. His memorandum gives the Polish case in a Polish voice, a rare thing in a volume of American papers. Readers should weigh it as the plea of a man who knew his country was being decided by others.
frus-1945-50-intel-d85:
Russell sent Secretary Byrnes a formal report on 12 February 1946. Reports from an administration chief sum up a period and recommend a course. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By February the new central group existed, and the State Department had to fix its own intelligence office's size and duties beside it. Russell's report belongs to that fixing. Readers can trace in it the department's retreat from its autumn ambition to house the nation's analysts. The report is the kind of paper on which offices are cut: measured, factual, and fatal. The volume's State thread bends here toward the office's transfer out of the department's heartland.
frus-1945-50-intel-d185:
The meeting named in the title took place on 12 February 1947, and these minutes are its formal record. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 185 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d285:
Dated 7 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Lay) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 285 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d385:
On 7 July 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 43d Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 385 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. With the Dulles Report now public inside the government, agencies were sorting out what to change and what to defend.

A memcon lets later readers sit in on a talk they could not attend: who spoke, what was asked, what was left open. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1861-d85:
Writing on 25 September 1861, William H. Seward counseled patience in a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 85 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late September found the war at a standstill in the East. Seward's letters abroad grew more plain and more patient. This one kept Adams to the long game in London: hold the line, make no threats, and let time work for the Union. Time, Seward judged, fought for the side that could feed and fund its armies. Letting time work was a plan that asked much of men's nerves, and Seward had them.
frus-1861-d185:
A second letter from the Acting Secretary of State to Carl Schurz bears the date 5 November 1861. It is document 185 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters to Madrid in one day from the acting chief match the Secretary's own habit. Each takes its own point in the Spanish file. The pair falls days before the Trent seizure, in the last calm week of the autumn. Last calm weeks in this file are few, and this pair of letters marks one. Few calm weeks remained in 1861, and the file soon shows why.
frus-1861-d285:
By the date of 19 August 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Haldeman. Congress received it as Document 285 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d85:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 26 June 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 85 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d185:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London on 10 November 1862. Opening a run of four same-day letters printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Documents 185 through 188.

Four letters in one mail marks a desk-clearing day at the State Department, with a steamer waiting. The topics would have ranged over the whole London brief, from British politics to ships building for the South. This first letter of the set starts a batch that, read whole, gives Washington's position in mid-November in unusual detail. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d285:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 6 June 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 285 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter followed a Dayton report by one day in the file.

Early June brought the Union victory at Memphis on the Mississippi, news that traveled fast and impressed shipowners and bankers in Europe. Seward's dispatches often carried such facts to his envoys as arguments. A letter like this one let Dayton walk into the French foreign ministry with fresh proof that the Union was winning the river war. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d385:
On 28 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Simon Cameron a dispatch printed as Document 385 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia, at St. Petersburg.

Late July 1862 was a season of Union setbacks, and letters to St. Petersburg took the longest road in the Department's mail. Seward wrote knowing his words would be read a month later, in a different military world. Dispatches to Russia therefore favored lasting lines over daily news, a quality that marks this channel's papers. The czar's government had freed its own serfs in 1861 and watched America's struggle closely.
frus-1862-d485:
On 27 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to James Shepherd Pike in The Hague. The instruction is Document 485 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Three weeks had passed since Seward's last Dutch order, and the war news in them was good: Fort Donelson had fallen. Good news was a diplomatic asset, and Seward spent it promptly, sending his ministers the facts to use at court. Pike's work in the Netherlands also touched Dutch colonial ports in the Caribbean, where belligerent ships might seek entry. The letter shows Washington feeding a small post the material it needed to hold its ground.
frus-1862-d585:
On 28 March 1862 Thomas Corwin sent a further report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 585 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Three Corwin reports in eight days mark March 1862 as a turning point in Mexico. Spain and Britain were preparing to withdraw. France would be left to press on alone. Corwin's letters home caught that shift as it happened. They weighed what it meant for the United States. That country was then too busy with its own rebellion to do more than protest. The file is the nearest thing the volume offers to a front-line diplomatic diary, written by a veteran statesman in a capital under foreign threat.
frus-1862-d685:
On 8 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Sydney Thayer, the American consul general in Egypt. The letter is document 685 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It answers the run of reports Thayer had sent from Alexandria.

Seward's outward mail told consuls what Washington wanted watched and how far they could go. For Egypt, trade and the safety of Americans on the Nile route sat high on the list. This letter shows the State Department guiding a lone post on a busy sea road. In the same weeks, it fought to keep Europe out of the Civil War.
frus-1863p1-d85:
A cluster of same-date letters opens with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 19 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London, and Adams letters of the same date sit right after this one in the volume. The letter is document 85 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote in a week when the two men's pens would cross once more. His letters fed Adams the facts and the tone for talks with the British foreign office. This one opens a same-date cluster in the file. Read with the Adams sheets that share its date, it shows both ends of the sea mail working at once. Each end was in the dark about the other's page.
frus-1863p1-d185:
An instruction dated 5 May 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 185 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d285:
The State Department's mail for London dated 5 September 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 285 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d385:
A formal note dated 7 February 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 385 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d485:
Dated 29 April 1863, document 485 is a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d585:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 14 July 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d685:
On 10 November 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter is printed as document 685 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official set of American diplomatic papers.

Seward and Lyons dealt with each other often, and their calm tone helped keep a hard tie steady. Britain stayed out of the war, but strains over ships, ports, and seized goods kept coming up. A note like this one did the daily work of that tie. It shows how big aims, such as keeping peace with Britain, rested on short, clear, polite words.
plos-pone-0000085:
Jeffery P. Demuth, Tijl De Bie, Jason E. Stajich, and their team traced gene families across mammals in PLOS ONE in 2006. A gene family grows when genes are copied and shrinks when copies are lost. Comparing family sizes across mammal genomes shows which families expanded in which lines.

Some families ballooned in just one branch, often those tied to smell, immunity, or reproduction, where fast change pays. Others stayed near constant for a hundred million years. That mix reveals the tempo of genome change: mostly slow drift, with bursts where life history demands. The mammal-wide map gives later studies a baseline for judging whether any one family's change is special.
plos-pone-0000185:
Krishna Jafa, Pragna Patel, Duncan A. MacKellar, and colleagues published this HIV testing study in PLOS ONE in 2007. In 2004 the OraQuick test became the first rapid HIV antibody test approved in the US for oral fluid. It gives results in 20 minutes without a blood draw. The authors investigated false positive results reported with it from August 2004 to June 2005.

A false positive tells a healthy person they may have HIV, so clusters of them demand investigation. The team traced where and why the errors occurred. Their report helped testing programs judge when a rapid result needs lab confirmation, protecting trust in a test designed for fast, wide use.
plos-pone-0000285:
Jenny Fredriksson, Dragi Anevski, Peter Almgren, and colleagues published this human genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. GYS1 is a gene for making glycogen, the stored form of sugar in muscle. The authors report that variation in GYS1 interacts with exercise and gender to predict cardiovascular mortality, the risk of dying from heart and vessel disease.

A gene's effect may only appear in people who exercise, or in one sex. Testing for such interactions keeps researchers from missing real risk factors by averaging everyone together. The finding is a case study in why genetic risk cannot always be read from DNA alone.
plos-pone-0000385:
Dirk Taubert and colleagues studied a molecular gateway in human cells in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. OCT2 is a transporter, a protein that carries small charged molecules across cell membranes. It is known for handling drugs and waste, but the team asked which of the body's own chemicals it normally carries.

Identifying OCT2's natural substrates showed a link to dopamine-using nerve cells, the kind lost in Parkinson's disease. A transporter that moves dopamine-related chemicals could affect how those neurons handle their signals and toxins. The work connects a kidney-and-liver transport protein to brain chemistry, widening where researchers might look for disease mechanisms.
plos-pone-0000485:
Soon-Lim Shin and colleagues found rhythm in the firing of cerebellar neurons, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Purkinje cells are the main output neurons of the cerebellum, the brain structure that fine-tunes movement. Their simple spike trains, the streams of signals they emit, were long read as irregular; the team reported regular patterns in them.

Regularity in a spike train can carry information that average firing rates miss, such as precise timing for coordinating muscles. Showing that cerebellar output has pattern challenges models that treat it as noisy. The work supports a view of the cerebellum as a timing machine, where when a cell fires matters as much as how often.
plos-pone-0000585:
Adrienne Anginot and colleagues showed how immune cells and one adaptor protein govern bone-eating cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Osteoclasts dissolve bone, and their overactivation causes bone loss. The team found that lymphocytes and the Dap12 adaptor are key regulators of osteoclast activation. The activation studied was the kind linked to gonadal failure. That is the hormone drop that drives postmenopausal bone loss.

Bone biology and immunology meet in this finding: immune cells help set how aggressively bone is resorbed when estrogen falls. Dap12 is a signaling adaptor in immune cells, making it a possible drug handle. The work helps explain why menopause thins bone and where treatment might intervene.
plos-pone-0000685:
Andrew Orr, Marie-Pierre Dubé, Julien Marcadier and colleagues pinned a rare eye disease on one gene, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy is a rare inherited disease passed in dominant fashion. The cornea slowly clouds as lipids build up locally. Some cases also come with abnormal blood lipids across the body.

Earlier studies had narrowed the search but not closed it. The title states the conclusion: mutations in the UBIAD1 gene, which encodes a possible prenyltransferase, are causal for the disease. Naming the gene enables genetic testing for families, and it directs research at the lipid chemistry that clouds the cornea.
plos-pone-0000785:
Shripad D. Tuljapurkar, Cedric O. Puleston and Michael D. Gurven argued that men's mating patterns help explain why humans live so long. Evolutionary theory predicts senescence, declining survival with age, because selection acts more strongly on genes affecting early fertility and mortality than on late ones. Hamilton had quantified that argument: a rare mutation reducing late survival spreads easily because selection barely notices it.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title flips the lens: mating patterns drive the evolution of human lifespan, and men matter in that math. If older males can still reproduce, selection keeps working on late-life survival. Long human life, including post-reproductive years, may partly be a by-product of male fertility.
plos-pone-0000885:
Maira Goytia, Nathalie Chamond, Alain Cosson and co-authors compared two closely related enzymes from harmful germs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One enzyme, proline racemase, comes from the parasite that causes Chagas disease. It is a confirmed drug target because the parasite needs it to live and spread in its host.

The puzzle is that a near twin enzyme, hydroxyproline epimerase, does a slightly different job. Mixing the two up could mislead drug design. The team set out the molecular and structural marks that separate them. Clear marks like these help chemists aim at the parasite enzyme without hitting the wrong target.
plos-pone-0000985:
Suresh Gopalan described controls acting across cells that limit a plant virus in Arabidopsis, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Viruses infect many hosts, and how hosts and viruses signal during infection is still being mapped. That mapping should help design ways to prevent disease.

Gopalan reports a multidirectional non-cell autonomous control, meaning resistance signals act beyond the infected cell, plus a genetic interaction that restricts tobacco etch virus susceptibility. Plants cannot run from infection, so internal signaling is their whole defense strategy. Work in Arabidopsis, the standard lab plant, often transfers to crops. A control that works across cells is a promising kind of resistance.
plos-pone-0001085:
Jing Qu, Guang-Hui Liu, Kaiyuan Wu and colleagues showed that nitric oxide destabilizes a protein that controls sumoylation, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sumoylation is a tagging system that adjusts how proteins work after they are built. How the tagging pathway itself is regulated was largely unknown.

The team report nitric oxide causes global hyposumoylation, a broad drop in SUMO tags, by destabilizing Pias3. Nitric oxide is a gas cells use as a quick signal, so linking it to a whole tagging system gives it wide reach. One small molecule turning down a general adjustment system could reshape many proteins at once during inflammation or nerve signaling.
plos-pone-0001185:
Pitcher plants of the genus Nepenthes catch insects in jug-shaped leaves filled with digestive fluid. Laurence Gaume and Yoel Forterre studied a surprising property of that fluid in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The plants, widespread in the Asian tropics, live on nutrients from the arthropods they trap.

The authors describe the fluid as viscoelastic. It acts partly like a liquid and partly like an elastic solid, and they show it is deadly to prey. That stickiness helps explain why insects that land in the fluid fail to escape even when it is diluted by rain. The work reveals a trapping mechanism quite different from a simple drowning pool.
plos-pone-0001285:
El Niño events periodically warm the Pacific and starve the Galápagos of food, and marine iguanas suffer heavily. Sebastian Steinfartz and colleagues measured the genetic impact of a severe El Niño on these iguanas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation is a major source of climatic disturbance for ecosystems worldwide.

The authors examined how a severe event reshaped the genetic makeup of Amblyrhynchus cristatus populations, through deaths and breeding skews. Models predict stronger and more frequent El Niño events as greenhouse gases rise. Genetic data from past events show what future ones may do to island species.
plos-pone-0001385:
Stephen Welle, Rabi Tawil, and Charles Thornton published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on why men's muscles are larger than women's. The gap in muscle mass is plain to see, but its gene basis was not clear. The team set out to find genes that might drive the gap. They compared gene use in muscle samples from men and women.

By reading which genes were on or off in each sex, they built a list of leads. Some genes stood out as much more active in one sex than the other. The list gives a base for work on muscle growth, loss, and sex based gaps in muscle ills. It may also inform care for weak or wasting muscle.
plos-pone-0001485:
David Allen and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on norovirus, a top cause of stomach flu in all ages. Human noroviruses come in many types, and one type rules world wide. The team read changes in one part of its shell protein. They asked which changes mark each strain and draw immune attack.

Their map of change in that shell region flags spots that likely act as strain marks. Antibodies aim at those spots, so change there lets the virus dodge past defense. Tracking such spots helps labs spot new strains early. It also informs the hard quest for a norovirus shot.
plos-pone-0001585:
Amelia Turagabeci, Keiko Nakamura, and Takehito Takano published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on healthy habits and youth harm in Japan. Bullying, violence, and injury are grave school ills for teens. Daily habits such as sound food, hygiene, and exercise anchor school health plans. The team asked whether those habits track with less harm.

They found teens with healthier daily habits faced lower risks of being bullied, of violence, and of injury. A habits link gives schools a low cost lever beyond rules and guards. It also ties body health to social safety in a way plans can use. The data come from a broad youth survey.
plos-pone-0001685:
Elza Rakhimova, Antje Munder, Lutz Wiehlmann, and their co-authors studied shape-changing bacteria in infected airways for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes chronic lung infections, above all in cystic fibrosis. During long infections, one founding clone splits into niche specialists and varied colony shapes, a pattern called dissociative behavior.

The authors tested how fit these isogenic colony variants are, meaning strains that differ only in colony form. They used a mouse airway infection model to compare them. The full text gives the variant types, the infection results, and which forms held up best in the lung. Knowing which shapes thrive in airways helps explain how this germ settles in for years despite treatment.
plos-pone-0001785:
Keith W. Sockman examined how hatching order shapes a young bird's chances in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dependent siblings compete for food their parents provide, and that competition can kill. The probability of death may depend partly on production order: eggs laid later hatch later, leaving chicks smaller than their siblings. In altricial birds, chicks hatch helpless and stay in the nest.

Sockman reports that ovulation order mediates a trade-off between survival before hatching and survival after it. The full text gives the nest records and the survival patterns by laying position. The trade-off shows parents and evolution balancing two risks at once, and it explains why laying order effects differ among bird studies.
plos-pone-0001885:
Hanna Maenpaa and co-authors ran a trial on thyroid cancer care in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. After surgery to remove the thyroid, patients often get radioactive iodine to burn away any tissue left behind. How much iodine to give was unsettled, so the team set up a randomized test of a low dose against a high dose.

The trial enrolled one hundred sixty adults whose cancer was of the papillary or follicular type. Each person got one of the two dose levels, and the team judged how well the leftover tissue was cleared. Dose choice matters: too much adds risk and cost, too little may leave tissue behind. Trials like this set the dose on proof, not habit.
plos-pone-0001985:

The team found that levels of this signal rose with influenza A infection. As the title states, infection activates this pro-inflammatory pathway. A signal that flares in flu may help explain why some cases turn severe. It also gives drug work a new point to calm the response.

mccrindle-ancient-india-ptolemy-1885:
McCrindle translated Ptolemy's geographical account of India in 1885. Ptolemy, the Alexandrian astronomer and mapmaker, surveyed the subcontinent around 150 CE. His Geography assigned coordinates to hundreds of Indian places.

Ports, rivers, tribes, and trade roads each receive a place on the grid. McCrindle's notes identify ancient names with modern sites across India. The result is the ancient world's most exact look at the subcontinent. Merchants' reports from the Roman sea trade fed Ptolemy's information. Errors exist, including a badly stretched east coast, but the ambition impresses. Scholars of ancient trade still mine McCrindle's Ptolemy for evidence about routes.
bailly-report-franklin-commissioners-eng:
The Franklin commission's report on animal magnetism reached English readers in this London translation of 1785. Jean-Sylvain Bailly had drafted the French original in 1784. Franklin, Lavoisier, and Guillotin stood among the commissioners who tested Mesmer's claimed fluid and found nothing there.

English readers now got the famous verdict firsthand. The cures, the report argued, came from imagination, not from any magnetic fluid. Careful blind trials backed the claim. The translation carried the Enlightenment's most famous no across the Channel within a year. It remains a model of how to test a marvel claim fairly, then report the result plainly.
sinclair-satans-invisible-world-english-:
George Sinclair, a Scottish professor of philosophy, published Satan's Invisible World Discovered in 1685. The book is a choice collection of relations, accounts offered as proof of spirits, witches, and apparitions. It became the Scottish classic against Sadducism, the doubt of the spirit world.

Sinclair gathers Scottish cases with names and places attached. Witches, ghosts, and second sight all testify in his pages. His purpose is polemical, but his relish for a good story shows through. Northern ghost lore here marches under a professor's banner. The collection preserves tales that might else have vanished. It also shows Scotland answering the skeptics in kind, story for sworn story.
three-distinct-knocks-1785:
The Three Distinct Knocks first appeared in London in 1760 as an exposé of the most antient Free-Masonry. This Dublin reprint of 1785 carried the Irish edition across the water. The book gives the fullest eighteenth-century printed ritual of the three degrees, with the opening and closing of lodges in working order.

Its title names the raps that announce a candidate at the lodge door. Inside, catechisms carry the whole Craft system degree by degree. Irish Masonry had its own strong life, and the Dublin printing served it. Historians rank the Knocks beside Jachin and Boaz among the great exposures. For the ritual as actually worked in the period, few printed sources run fuller.
